runs.text: Made by Arshad · 28-fund review
Where each of the 28 funds stands

Nine funds are heavily exposed to an AI-led sell-off, but AI is not the only threat. Oil lurching on every Iran headline (about $92 on 19 Nov, down from $115 in late October), a yen at almost 160 per dollar, the level that has triggered intervention, a 10-year US yield back above 5% with a December Fed hike close to certain, and rising tension around Taiwan each hit different funds. Combining all of these, 11 funds rate High or Very high overall risk. Only the money market funds and cash are close to safe in every scenario.
Why these 28:

together they form a comprehensive set covering cash in three currencies, government and corporate bonds, developed and emerging-market shares, real estate, commodities, gold and absolute return, across the US, Europe, the UK, Japan, Asia and the Pacific. Almost any market event shows up somewhere in the list.

US Treasuries (28) and the global bond funds (9, 25, 26) should rise if a crash pushes the Fed to cut. They fell this year because war-driven inflation pushed yields up, so they guard against a growth shock, not an inflation shock.

The yen funds (11, 27) are a currency bet with the yen near ¥158. The commodity fund (12) would fall if an Iran deal reopens Hormuz. Europe (5) is exposed to French debt stress, and the Asian funds (22, 23, 24) to Taiwan tension and currency outflows.

Update · Fri 20 Nov 2026, 6 am Manila (covers Thu 19 Nov)
Anthropic jumps 17% on its debut, but the S&P 500 falls 2% for a sixth day, 8.2% below its record

Anthropic's record listing went well. Priced at $83 a share, it raised $81.3bn, opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17, up 17%. But it did not lift the market. An early rally faded, and the S&P 500 fell 2.0% to 7,175.83, its sixth straight fall and 8.2% below its record. The Dow lost 1,101 points and the Nasdaq 2.3%, as AMD and NVIDIA slid. Fed Governor Waller pushed for aggressive action in December. Gold fell about 2% to a 14-month low, another blow to the gold-miners fund, and Taiwan fell about 4.4%. No fund rating changed.

cells.text: What happened
Funds affected
What it means
Anthropic's record IPO: a strong start that faded.

It priced 980 million shares at $83, above its $70–78 guide, raising a record $81.3bn (Yahoo Finance, Reuters via Kitco). The shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the offer price and worth over $1.5tn, then slid back to close at $97.17, up 17.1%, and eased to about $95.7 after hours (Yahoo Finance).

Strong demand shows investors still want AI growth at the right price, and a flop was avoided. But the fade from the open, and a big new supply of AI shares, did nothing for the AI-heavy equity funds (6, 3, 4, 13, 19).
Wall Street fell 2% for a sixth straight day.

The S&P 500 had been up as much as 1.3% early, but closed down 2.0% (148 points) at 7,175.83, below its 5 Nov low of 7,354. The Dow fell 2.2% (1,101 points) to 49,097.06 and the Nasdaq 2.3% to 23,879.20 (Yahoo Finance). AP called it the longest S&P losing streak in about two and a half years, with more than 90% of S&P stocks lower late in the day. NVIDIA rose as much as 4.7% early, then fell about 2–3%; AMD fell about 7–10% after a short-seller's report (sources differ); Walmart slipped about 1% despite results slightly above forecasts. The VIX fear gauge jumped about 14% to 27.98 (AP, Yahoo Finance, Reuters via Kitco).

The broad equity funds (6, 3, 4, 13, 19), the multi-asset funds (17, 18) and real estate (2) fell again. The S&P 500 is now 8.2% below its record, about 1.9% above the −10% level (~7,040). The market is now falling on the broad AI worry rather than on single results.
Fed: Waller wants aggressive action.

Governor Waller told CNBC the Fed needs either a half-point hike in December or guidance for more hikes (Reuters via The Star). Markets put about 90% odds on a quarter point and about 8–10% on half a point (Reuters via Kitco, Trading Economics). Jobless claims rose slightly and Mid-Atlantic factory growth slowed more than forecast. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.05% from 5.07% (AP). The dollar index reached a 19-month high of about 103.9 (Reuters via The Star).

A December hike is still close to certain. Government bond funds (28, 26, 25, 9) held steady as yields edged down on weak stocks; corporate bond funds (20, 21) face wider spreads if the sell-off spreads. Cash and USD money market funds (10, 14) keep earning more.
Gold hit a 14-month low; oil stayed near three-month lows.

Gold fell about 2% to roughly $3,665 an ounce (futures), below $3,700 for the first time since September 2025, as the dollar firmed on Fed hike bets (Yahoo Finance, Trading Economics). Brent was about $92 a barrel, near its lowest since late August and down about 20% this month, and US crude ended near $83, up about 1% (Reuters via The Star, Trading Economics, Yahoo Finance). Reports said Trump is considering more strikes on Iran (Trading Economics).

The gold-miners fund (1) takes another hit: miners usually fall further than gold itself. Commodities (12) stay soft with oil and gold, and the UK fund (8), with its big oil companies, gets little help.
Taiwan slumped; Japan and Korea held up.

Taiwan's market fell about 4.4% in afternoon trading and the MSCI Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index lost 1.7% to a seven-month low, heading for a weekly fall of almost 6%, its steepest since early March (Reuters via The Star). Japan's Nikkei rose 0.7% to 59,443.99 and Korea's KOSPI 1.4% to 5,137.89, helped by SoftBank (+4.6%) and SK Hynix (TradingKey, AP). The yen was about 159.5 per dollar, the euro about $1.096 and the Australian dollar at a 10-month low after weak jobs data (Reuters via The Star). Germany's DAX fell about 1.1% (AP).

The Asian equity funds (24, 22) lost ground with Taiwan's chipmakers, and Asian currencies (23) stay under pressure from a strong dollar. Japan (27) held up, but the yen near 160 keeps intervention risk high for the yen fund (11). A weak Australian dollar hurts Pacific (7) in dollar terms, and Europe (5) slipped.
Coming up (Manila):

Any outcome from Trump's talks with Xi and Putin in China, including on Iran; Bessent's deadline for NVIDIA's board around 25 Nov; OPEC+ meeting on 2027 output 29 Nov; Jensen Huang asked to testify to the Senate on 3 Dec, US time; US November jobs report Fri 4 Dec, 9:30 pm; Fed decision 8–9 Dec, US time.
The Fed and the jobs report matter most for the bond funds (28, 9); Iran and OPEC+ for commodities (12) and gold miners (1); NVIDIA's leadership for the equity funds (6, 19).

Earlier updates
NVIDIA beat forecasts but its shares fell; the S&P 500 dropped for a fifth day, 6.4% below its record.

On 17 Nov the Dow fell 1.6%, software stocks led the losses, US retail sales beat forecasts and a December Fed hike was about 95% priced. No change.

The chip index fell about 4.6% and Taiwan about 6%, while Brent fell 3.6% to $92.44 on the IEA's surplus forecast. No change.
Iran said a supertanker sank in Hormuz and its drones targeted Bahrain; NVIDIA results and Anthropic's debut lined up a decisive week.
Over the weekend Saudi Arabia intercepted Houthi missiles and drones and the G7 condemned Iran's attacks; Brent had closed Friday near $96. No change.

In Friday afternoon trading on 13 Nov the chip index was down about 3.7%, AMD about 10.6% and the S&P 500 about 0.5–0.8%, and the 10-year yield touched 5.17%. No change.
NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang resigned; oil jumped as Trump said no Iran deal is needed.
On 12 Nov NVIDIA fell as much as 14% and closed about 4.3% lower, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,592, and the 10-year yield rose to about 5.1%. No change.
Chip stocks bounced back as CoreWeave calmed AI-spending fears.
On 11 Nov the chip index rose about 7% and the S&P 500 about 1.3% to roughly 7,620, with NVIDIA up about 3.5%. Brent rose about 1% to $92.5 as Iran denied talks. No change.
Hotter US inflation pushed the 10-year yield back above 5%, and NVIDIA sank.

On 10 Nov October consumer prices rose 0.4% in the month, making a December Fed hike close to fully priced. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,520 and NVIDIA fell 5.5–6.3% (sources differ), after Asia had rallied. No change.
Wall Street jumped 2.3% as chips rebounded and oil sank, but NVIDIA fell on a probe of its CEO.
On 9 Nov the S&P 500 rose to 7,550 and the chip index about 7%, while NVIDIA fell 4.4% and Brent dropped to about $93–94. No change.
Asia opened split, then Korea turned higher.
The Nikkei opened 2% higher while the KOSPI briefly fell below 5,000 on foreign selling, then recovered to 5,113 as SK Hynix and Samsung rebounded. Brent eased to about $97. No change.
A partial bounce: chips +4%, a strong US jobs report, and oil's biggest weekly fall since 2020.

On 6 Nov the chip index rose 4.2% and the S&P 500 0.3% to 7,377, but Asia had already slumped (Nikkei −6.0%, KOSPI −6.0%). US jobs beat forecasts, lifting December hike odds to about 77%, and Brent ended the week near $98. No change.
AI meltdown: Nasdaq −5.5% into correction, chip index −12% in a day.

On 5 Nov the S&P 500 fell 4.4% to 7,354, NVIDIA 9.3% and AMD about 15%; Korea's KOSPI fell 5.3% and the Nikkei broke below 60,000. Treasuries rallied, and the Bank of England raised rates to 4.00%. No change.
After the US election: stocks rallied, oil fell below $95, AI-infrastructure stocks slid.

News reports said Democrats won both houses of Congress. The Dow rose 3.0%, its best day of 2026, and Brent fell 8.7% to $94.62. NVIDIA fell 3.2% and CoreWeave 9.9% on data-centre policy worries. No change.
Oil fell 7.6% on Iran deal hopes, and AI stocks kept sliding.
Brent fell to $104.77; US "defensive strikes" hit Qeshm Island. Oracle filed to raise $20bn for AI. The RBA hiked to 4.85% (6–3 vote). No change.
Weekend: an Iran deal or new strikes both looked closer.
Doha talks continued, and a draft US–Iran framework was reported. No change.
The AI sell-off spread on Friday, and gold fell with it.
The Nasdaq-100 fell 3.5%, Intel 29%. Gold hit a one-year low of $3,899. A tanker was hit by limpet mines in Hormuz.
Big Tech cracked.
Alphabet fell 12.6%, its worst day ever, and Amazon fell after hours on a miss. The ECB held. No change.
Alphabet's miss is the clearest AI-bubble warning yet.
The Fed held 10–2, and the UK Budget doubled the bank surcharge. No change.

AI-crash scenario
Who gets hurt, who holds

In an AI-led crash I estimate the most AI-concentrated funds could fall 30–40%, broad developed-market equity funds 20–30%, and cash would hold its value. Government bonds would likely gain a few percent, but only if the crash lowers inflation fears rather than arriving with another oil shock.

My estimates from each fund's AI concentration, equity beta and volatility, calibrated to the 2000–02 dot-com bust (S&P 500 about −49%), 2022 (MSCI World −18%, US Treasuries −13%) and Korea's July 2026 chip crash (KOSPI −40% in six weeks). Not forecasts.
Scenario assumed.

AI capital spending is cut sharply, US mega-cap tech falls 40–50%, the S&P 500 falls 25–35% and Asian chip stocks repeat their July 2026 slide. The Fed responds by cutting rates. If inflation stays high instead (for example, the Strait of Hormuz closes again), the bond funds would not rise and only cash would hold.
Liquidity.
Every fund deals daily; settlement is typically 1–3 business days plus any platform processing time. In a crash the practical risks are:
Emerging-market and Asian equity funds (22, 24) and the commodity swap fund (12) can see prices gap and dealing spreads widen.
Funds can apply swing pricing or, in extreme cases, defer large redemptions; this matters most for the active and EM funds.
Selling after a fall locks in the loss. The 2000–02 and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rebounds that punished late sellers.
Ranking by safety, lowest risk first

Goldman Sachs Yen Liquid Reserves (11): stable in yen; a currency position for USD-based investors.

L&G Diversified (17, 18): about half equity.
UK (8), Europe ex-UK (5), Pacific (7): equities with low AI exposure.
Real estate (2), Japan (27), commodities (12): moderate to high volatility with partial AI or rate exposure.
Developed World (3, 4), NT Climate (19), North America (6): broad but AI-heavy.
Robeco EM (22), HSBC Islamic (13), Schroder Asian Opportunities (24), World Gold miners (1): the most volatile; the first three are the most AI-exposed of the 28 funds.
Beyond AI
Eight other risks in the news now, and which funds they hit
An AI crash is one way to lose money; these are the others. Several are already moving markets this month. Numbers link to each fund's analysis.
Green
marks a fund that would likely benefit.
1 · Yen turmoil

The yen fell to about 163 per dollar in late July, prompting a joint US–Japan intervention (Japan reportedly spent around $85bn) that pushed it to 155. By mid-August most of that gain had reversed. It was near 158 on 27 Oct, and Finance Minister Katayama has warned she is ready to act again, with traders watching 160. In the week to 6 Nov the dollar traded between about 157.3 and 158.8 yen; hawkish Bank of Japan minutes and the stock rout helped the yen, but the strong US jobs report pushed the dollar back to the mid-158s. The pressures are a slow Bank of Japan (held at 1.25% on 30 Oct, though it signalled more hikes), PM Takaichi's 19 Oct signal that about ¥10 trillion of tax cuts may be funded with deficit bonds (debt is 204% of GDP), 10-year JGB yields near 3%, and an oil import bill that has only just started to ease (Brent near $98 on 6 Nov, from $115 in late October). On 12–13 Nov the dollar reached about 159.8–159.9 yen, the closest yet to 160. On 16 Nov it was near 159.6 after Japan reported that its economy shrank at a 0.1% annual rate in July–September. On 17 Nov it eased to about 159.2. On 18 Nov it held near 159.3, and on 19 Nov it was about 159.5 as the dollar index hit a 19-month high. The move can run either way: intervention or a carry-trade unwind could lift the yen 5% in days.

2 · Oil shock and the Strait of Hormuz

Brent settled at $115.32 on 28 Oct, about 75% higher than a year ago. After the 3 Nov US election it fell sharply, ending the week of 6 Nov at $98.32. On 10 Nov it briefly fell below $90 for the first time since August after Trump said the war was militarily effectively over. On 16 Nov Brent fell 3.6% to $92.44 even as Iran targeted Bahrain again, as the IEA forecast a surplus of about 1.7 million barrels a day this quarter. On 17 Nov Brent rose about 1% to around $93.50 after Iranian drones hit a US radar system in Bahrain and a ship in the strait was hit twice, though it is still about 20% lower this month. On 18 Nov US crude fell about 3–4% to roughly $82 and Brent was near $92 at midday after a surprise 3.4-million-barrel rise in US crude stocks, even as Iran reportedly attacked US sites in Kuwait after a US strike on Qeshm Island. On 19 Nov Brent held near $92, close to a three-month low, amid reports that Trump is considering more strikes on Iran. Nothing is agreed, and the strait has been largely closed since March. This is a two-way risk. A deal could send oil sharply lower; Brent fell to about $72 during the brief June truce. A longer closure keeps inflation and rates high.

3 · Sticky inflation and rising bond yields

US CPI rose to 3.7% in September (core 2.6%). The Fed held on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a hike. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35%, the highest since 2002. On 10 Nov October CPI rose 0.4% in the month (core 0.3%), above forecasts; the 10-year yield jumped to about 5.01%, a December hike became close to fully priced, and Fed Governor Waller said a half-point move could be considered. On 17 Nov St. Louis Fed President Musalem said hikes may be needed sooner rather than later, and CME odds of a December hike were about 95%. On 18 Nov minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect a December hike, two floated half a point, and most worry inflation will persist; Waller said a quarter-point December move would need a signal of another in January. The 10-year yield eased to about 5.05–5.07% as oil fell. On 13 Nov producer prices were 6.5% higher than a year earlier, the most since 2022. On 19 Nov Waller said the Fed needs either a half-point December hike or guidance for more; markets put about 90% odds on a quarter point, and the 10-year yield held near 5.05%. Rising yields hurt bonds, REITs and expensive growth stocks at the same time, as in 2022.

4 · French debt stress and a weaker euro

France's 10-year yield hit 4.98% on 21 Oct, a 24-year high, and its spread over Germany reached 157 bp, the widest since the euro crisis. EUR/USD fell 3.9% between 9 Sep and 23 Oct even though the ECB raised rates twice this year to 2.50%. Eurozone inflation is 3.8%, and the October PMI fell to a four-month low. On 29 Oct the ECB held, the euro touched a 17-month low, and Lagarde's early exit (7 Feb 2027, before the French election) was confirmed. On 18 Nov the euro fell to about $1.096, its lowest since April 2025. On 19 Nov it stayed near $1.096, and Germany's DAX fell about 1.1%.

5 · Taiwan tension and Asian currency stress

China held live-fire drills across five sea areas on 12–17 Oct, coast-guard ships harassed Taiwanese vessels on 18 Oct, and on 16 Oct Beijing drafted export curbs on about 40 technologies, including AI and chips. On 15 Oct foreign investors sold NT$165bn of Taiwan stocks in one day, Korean outflows for October passed $10bn, the Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar for the first time, and India and Indonesia intervened to support their currencies. On 16 Nov the US tightened rules on Chinese access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centres, and Taiwan's market fell about 6%. On 17 Nov Taiwan fell another 2.3% and Korea's KOSPI 2.6% to a six-month low. On 18 Nov the KOSPI rebounded about 1.9% to back above 5,000, and Taiwan edged up 0.1%, after NVIDIA's results. On 19 Nov Taiwan fell about 4.4% and the MSCI Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index hit a seven-month low, while Korea rose 1.4%.

6 · AI debt inside "safe" bond funds

AI-related borrowing has passed roughly $466–500bn this year and makes up about 10% of the largest long-term investment-grade bond ETFs. Oracle's 5-year CDS more than doubled to about 308 bp, Meta's and NVIDIA's hit records in October, and CoreWeave's implies a default probability above 60%. Pimco as a firm bought $18bn of Meta's Hyperion data-centre bond. On 28 Oct Alphabet reported that its long-term debt had jumped from $46.5bn to $125.1bn in a year, alongside $12.4bn of stock sales, to pay for AI. On 2 Nov Oracle filed to sell $10bn of stock and $10bn of senior notes for the same purpose. After the 3 Nov election, analysts flagged Democrats' openness to data-centre moratoriums, and on 4 Nov AI-infrastructure names fell (NVIDIA −3.2%, CoreWeave −9.9%, Vistra −13.8%) even as the market rallied. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12.3% and the Nasdaq entered correction, as investors priced a slower, costlier AI build-out. On 11 Nov CoreWeave said it expects about $9bn of customer prepayments over three months and plans no more expensive debt through 2027; its shares jumped more than 20% and the chip index about 7%. On 19 Nov Anthropic raised a record $81.3bn in its IPO and its shares closed 17% above the $83 offer price, but CoreWeave swung from a 10.5% gain to a loss of about 5.5% as AI stocks slid again.

7 · UK Budget and gilts

The 10-year gilt yield touched 5.53% on 8 Oct, the highest since 2007. UK inflation is 3.5%, and markets expect a Bank of England hike on 5 Nov. The 28 Oct Budget kept about £15bn of fiscal headroom and gilts held steady, but it doubled the bank surcharge to 6%, a cost for the UK fund's banks. On 18 Nov UK inflation figures showed prices rising faster, and the 10-year gilt yield fell about 0.08 points to 5.29% as oil dropped.

8 · Gold's correction and Australia's rate hikes

Gold briefly fell below $4,000 on 23 Oct, about a quarter under its January record. It dropped alongside stocks as leveraged investors raised cash, so it did not behave as a safe haven that day. It slipped again on 29 Oct and fell 3.3% to a one-year low of $3,899 on 30 Oct as tech sold off, just above Standard Chartered's $3,886 warning level. It gained about 4.5% in the week to 6 Nov, its best week since August, ending near $4,050–4,080. On 12 Nov it fell about 2.9% to roughly $3,885 as the dollar firmed on Fed hike bets. On 18 Nov it fell about 3% to roughly $3,735–3,745, well below its 30 Oct low. On 19 Nov it fell about 2% to roughly $3,665 (futures), below $3,700 for the first time since September 2025. In Australia, the RBA has hiked four times this year to 4.60%, CPI is 4.0%, and Q3 core inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts on 28 Oct, and on 3 Nov the RBA hiked a fifth time to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, in a split 6–3 vote that dropped its tightening bias. On 19 Nov the Australian dollar hit a 10-month low after weak jobs data.

On 9 Nov Wall Street rebounded: the S&P 500 rose 2.3% and the chip index about 7%, while NVIDIA fell 4.4% on a board probe of its CEO and Brent dropped to about $93–94 (Reuters). On 10 Nov hotter October inflation (0.4% in the month) pushed the 10-year yield to about 5.01% and the S&P 500 down about 0.4%, with NVIDIA down 6.3%; Asia had rallied, with the KOSPI up 4% (AP). On 11 Nov chip stocks rebounded about 7% after CoreWeave's results, lifting the S&P 500 about 1.3% to roughly 7,620 (Reuters). On 12 Nov NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang resigned; NVIDIA fell as much as 14% before paring losses, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,592, and Brent rose after Trump said no Iran deal is needed (Kiplinger, AP). On 13 Nov chip stocks slid again (chip index about −3.4%, NVIDIA −2.0%) and the S&P 500 closed 0.4% lower at 7,561.67, but it still gained about 2.5% for the week, its first weekly gain in five; October producer prices were up 6.5% on a year, and the 10-year yield closed near 5.15% (Yahoo Finance, CappNotes). Over the weekend Iran said a supertanker sank after hitting a mine in the strait, and drone and missile attacks on Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were intercepted (AFP via RTÉ, Gulf News). On 16 Nov new US curbs on Chinese access to advanced chips sent the chip index down about 4.6% and the S&P 500 about 1.9% to roughly 7,415, more than 5% below its record, while Brent fell 3.6% to $92.44 on the IEA's surplus forecast (Reuters, Bloomberg). On 17 Nov stocks fell again before NVIDIA's results: the S&P 500 lost 1.2% to about 7,327, about 6.3% below its record, and Korea's KOSPI closed below 5,000 for the first time since February (Reuters, AP). On 18 Nov NVIDIA's revenue beat forecasts at $115.8bn, but its shares fell about 3%; the S&P 500 slipped about 0.3% for a fifth straight fall while the Dow lost about 1.2%, and US crude fell 3–4% and gold about 3% (Wealth Professional, Yahoo Finance, Bloomberg). On 19 Nov Anthropic's record $81.3bn IPO opened 34% above its $83 price and closed up 17%, but an early rally faded and the S&P 500 fell 2.0% to 7,175.83, a sixth straight loss and 8.2% below its record, while gold fell to a 14-month low (Yahoo Finance, AP).

In an inflationary environment stocks and bonds can fall together, as in 2022. If an AI crash instead triggers a growth scare and Fed cuts, Treasuries and high-quality bonds should rally. Which of those two worlds arrives decides whether the bond funds protect you; only the cash-like funds are safe in both.

If the S&P 500 falls 5%, 10% or 20%: which funds to add

A guide to which of the 28 funds tend to be worth adding as a sell-off deepens, using the S&P 500's fall from its 7,819 record (6 Oct 2026) as the trigger, because it is the market's main gauge. The idea is to add the steadier, low-AI funds first and the high-growth, AI-heavy funds only once they are much cheaper. Purchases are funded mainly from cash and from bonds that have risen. Where we are now: at the close on Thursday (19 Nov, US time) the S&P 500 was 7,175.83, about 8.2% below its record, so it is below the −5% level (~7,430), which it first crossed on 5 Nov. The −10% level (~7,040) is about 1.9% lower.

In an AI or growth crash, Treasuries usually rise, so selling some bonds to buy stocks works. In an oil or inflation shock, bonds may fall too: fund purchases from cash (14) instead, and consider trimming the commodity fund (12), which is likely to have risen.

AI-crash estimates
are my judgement, not model output or forecasts.
Volatility 1–7
(shown as "Risk 1–7" in the earlier version) is my rating on the familiar SRI scale for how much each fund's price swings; it is not the official KID rating.
Other key risks
are non-AI threats backed by news from 4–26 October 2026: currencies, oil, inflation and rates, sovereign debt, geopolitics and credit. Each is rated Low, Medium or High for that fund.
Overall risk

combines AI exposure, those other risks and volatility into one judgement, on a scale from Very low to Very high, for an investor whose spending currency is the US dollar. Funds 11 and 15 carry a note because their risk is much lower in their own currency. These ratings are my judgement and will change with the news; the dates to watch are listed under Other risks.
